newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour ahead on economy - Reuters/NOP poll.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour ahead on economy - Reuters/NOP poll.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party has taken its clearest lead yet on some of the key economic issues likely to figure in the campaign for the May 1 election, a Reuters poll published on Tuesday showed.
The survey, conducted by leading poll organisation NOP, found that 35 percent of voters now trust Labour more to manage the economy, against 26 percent backing the Conservatives.

NOP polled 1,065 voters across 52 parliamentary constituencies last Friday. The snapshot of opinion provides one of the strongest readings yet recorded for the Labour party on key economic issues just weeks ahead of the election.

Labour's nine-point lead on which party could be trusted most with economic management compares with a two-point Conservative lead on the question in the last Reuters/NOP poll conducted on February 21.

The poll will dent Prime Minister John Major's hopes that the ruling Conservatives will start to reap the benefits of what they describe as their successful economic management, as Britain enjoys a combination of low unemployment, inflation and interest rates.

The shift in opinion on the key question of economic management was most marked in one of the most influential electoral groups -- so-called "C2" skilled manual workers, many of whom deserted Labour for the Conservatives in the 1980s.

The poll found Labour enjoyed a huge 32-point lead on the question of economic management, scoring 45 percent against the Conservatives' 13 percent among C2 workers. In the February 21 poll Labour's lead on this question was just four points among this section of the electorate.

But managerial and professional workers in the AB socio-demographic groups still back the Conservatives on economic management by 47 percent to 26 percent, a margin of 21 percent but down from the 24 percent lead recorded in the last Reuters/NOP poll.

Labour's lead on economic management was marked among both men and women, and voters of all ages, in contrast to the earlier poll which showed women and voters over 35 years old backing the Conservatives on the issue.
Labour has been trying to shed its reputation as a tax-and-spend party and has pledged not to raise the main income tax rates during the next parliament if it wins the election.
The Reuters/NOP poll also asked voters under which party they would be better off, taking into account what they spend, taxes, and their income from work, benefits and pensions.
Labour again registered a clear lead with 39 percent of voters backing them against 25 percent for the Conservatives, suggesting Labour's efforts to reassure voters on taxes is paying dividends.

Again Labour's lead on this question was most marked in the skilled manual workers' group, with a reading of 50 percent against 15 percent backing the Conservatives. The Conservatives' only lead on the personal prosperity question was among professional and managerial workers, by a margin of 20 percent.

While the economy is performing strongly, voters appear reluctant to thank the Conservatives for the upturn and have warmed to Labour as its leadership moves away from the traditional tax-and-spend economic policies still favoured by many of its party activists.
